opus-5.5.text:
I think of them as playing complementary roles, almost like two halves of a brain. Large language models, and more broadly the vision-language models we've been building on, are very good at the high-level part: understanding what a person wants, using common sense about the world, breaking a task like "clean up the table" into steps. They've absorbed huge amounts of knowledge from internet data, and that's something robotics never had before. Previously, every robot had to learn everything from scratch.

But knowing *what* to do is different from knowing *how* to do it with a physical body. A language model has read about picking up a cup, but it has never felt the weight of one or dealt with the slip of a finger. Low-level motor control, balance, contact, dexterity, reacting in milliseconds: that's where reinforcement learning has been really powerful, especially with simulation. In my own work on legged locomotion, for example, we train policies in simulation with RL, through enormous amounts of trial and error, and then transfer them to real robots. That kind of embodied skill is hard to get from text alone.

There's also a newer and very interesting connection: RL is now central to improving language models themselves. The reasoning progress we've seen recently comes largely from RL on top of pretrained models. I think robotics will follow a similar path. You pretrain a large foundation model on lots of data, including internet data, human videos, and robot demonstrations, which gives you a good prior. Then you use RL, in simulation or in the real world, to refine it, letting the robot practice, discover what works, and go beyond what it imitated. Imitation gets you to human-level demonstrations at best; RL is how you exceed them.

So I don't see it as RL versus large models. The foundation model provides knowledge and generalization, and RL provides the grounding and self-improvement through interaction with the physical world. Combining them well is, I think, one of the most important open problems in robotics right now.

r001.rationale: The response calls language models the high-level part of the system and compares the models’ and RL’s roles to two halves of a brain.

r002.rationale: It identifies low-level motor control, balance, contact, and dexterity as areas where reinforcement learning is powerful.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the simplest way I'd put it is that large language models and reinforcement learning are solving two different halves of the problem, and robotics needs both.

Language models are extraordinarily good at the high-level part. They carry a huge amount of common sense about the world. If you tell a robot "clean up the kitchen," a language model can break that down: pick up the cups, put them in the sink, wipe the counter, and so on. It understands what objects are, what people typically want, and how to sequence tasks. Five years ago, getting that kind of semantic reasoning into a robot was basically impossible. Now it comes almost for free.

But a language model has never actually touched anything. It doesn't know how much force to apply when grasping a glass, how to keep a legged robot balanced when it steps on something unexpected, or how to recover when a plan fails halfway through. That low-level, physical, contact-rich control is where reinforcement learning shines. RL lets the robot learn by trial and error, usually in simulation at massive scale, and discover behaviors that are very hard for humans to hand-design. Our work on legged locomotion is a good example. The gaits that come out of RL are often more robust than anything we could have engineered by hand.

So the way I see the stack right now: the language model acts as the planner and the interface to humans, and RL provides the motor skills underneath. The LLM says "walk over there and pick that up," and RL policies are what actually make the legs move and the fingers close.

What's getting interesting is how the boundary between the two is blurring. We've started using language models to help the RL side directly. In one project we had an LLM write reward functions for RL, which was always one of the most tedious parts of the pipeline. In another we had the language model generate low-level motion patterns for a quadruped, essentially using its reasoning ability to shape how the robot moves. And on the other direction, RL is now being used to fine-tune the large models themselves, so the model learns from the robot's actual successes and failures in the physical world rather than only from internet text.

I think the long-term picture is one foundation model that does both, where language, vision, and action live in the same network, and RL becomes the mechanism that grounds that model in physical reality. We're not fully there yet. Data is still the bottleneck, and real-world robot data is expensive. But the combination is clearly the direction. Neither piece alone gets you a general-purpose robot.

r001.rationale: The response presents language models as handling high-level reasoning, task planning, sequencing, and human interaction, which conveys the robotic system’s high-level cognitive role.

r002.rationale: It identifies low-level physical control, including force, balance, and contact-rich actions, as where reinforcement learning is particularly effective.

astra-6.text:
I think reinforcement learning and large language models play complementary roles in robotics. A language model can help a robot understand what a person wants and break that request into steps. Reinforcement learning can help the robot learn how to carry out those steps through interaction and feedback.

For example, if you ask a robot to bring you a cup, understanding the request is only part of the problem. The robot also has to move toward the cup, grasp it, and keep it stable while carrying it. Those actions involve contact, balance, and uncertainty. Being able to describe an action doesn’t automatically mean being able to execute it.

So one useful approach is to let the language model guide the task and use learned control policies to perform the physical skills. But the connection has to work in both directions: the robot needs to report what happened, what it can actually do, and when something failed, so the plan can change. I see reinforcement learning as an important way to connect high-level reasoning with reliable behavior in the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response describes the language model as understanding requests, breaking them into steps, and guiding the task, which conveys a high-level cognitive role.

r002.rationale: It assigns learned control policies to physical skills and explains that reinforcement learning helps robots carry out actions involving contact, balance, and uncertainty.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they play complementary roles. A large language model can help a robot understand what a person wants, bring in general knowledge, and break a task into steps. Reinforcement learning can help turn those steps into physical behavior: how to move, how to make contact, and how to recover when something goes wrong.

For example, “bring me a cup” sounds simple, but it involves very different problems. Understanding the request and deciding where to look are different from grasping the cup without dropping it. That second part requires learning through interaction and feedback, where reinforcement learning is particularly useful.

The interesting question is how tightly we connect them. A language model’s plan has to be grounded in what the robot can actually do, and the robot’s experience should inform the plan. So I see reinforcement learning as an important part of making these models useful in the physical world.

r001.rationale: It describes the language model as handling understanding, general knowledge, and task planning, which communicates its high-level cognitive role.

r002.rationale: It says reinforcement learning helps produce physical behavior such as movement and contact, and is particularly useful for learning grasping through interaction and feedback.
